newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian miners clean up violent image for polls.
newsitem.headline: Romanian miners clean up violent image for polls.

text.p: Romanian miners, notorious for rampages through central Bucharest to denounce liberals and market reforms, have tried to clean up their image in the Balkan country's presidential elections.

Both ex-Communist incumbent Ion Iliescu and his centrist rival in Sunday's run-off, Emil Constantinescu, have devoted considerable efforts to courting their 200,000 votes -- if only to reconcile Romanians after the violence of the early 1990s.

Unanswered questions about who was behind two rampages -- one six months after the December 1989 revolution that toppled Communism and put Iliescu in power -- became campaign issues in both presidential and general elections.

"The rampages were provoked to compromise us, control and use us against other social groups and democratic forces," said Marin Condescu, leader of 160,000 gold, coal and iron miners. He has told his membership to vote for Constantinescu.
Constantinescu baldly accused Iliescu during television debates of encouraging the miners to descend on the capital to help him outmanouevre political rivals and slow reforms.
"This was the most despicable aspect of the Iliescu regime. All human rights were trampled underfoot," he said.
Iliescu denied the allegations. "I never called in the miners. On the contrary, I intervened to calm things down."
Condescu is quick to point out that his men had nothing to do with the havoc wrought by those who smashed public buildings and party headquarters. Nine people were killed.
But many Romanians fail to see the distinction, referring to miners en masse as "hooligans" or "cavemen".

In the first wave of violence in June 1990, miners in helmets and rubber boots targeted students and opposition parties. Computers, documents and furniture were hurled through smashed university and office windows.
Young people who had occupied a square for two months were savagely beaten, loaded into buses and detained for a week.

In September 1991, the miners returned, storming government offices and "restoring order" by occupying parliament. They demanded the resignation of reformist Prime Minister Petre Roman. Iliescu announced his departure two days later.
"These sad, but real episodes must be clarified through public debate and trials and those who caused them sentenced," Condescu said.
A parliamentary report and police investigators blamed the violence on Miron Cosma, leader of 40,000 coal miners from the Jiu valley. But no one was ever brought to account.

Cosma also appears anxious to burnish his own image. Donning a suit and tie, he ran for parliament this month in his Jiu Valley stronghold, but lost badly. He has issued no instructions to his members on Sunday's vote.
Iliescu made a clear pitch for miners' votes in the television debates, saying Romania could not afford to shut down uneconomic pits and import coal.
Constantinescu made a more impassioned appeal to understand the miners' ethic and their needs.

"They have a brutal nature. They are tough. but they have their dignity. Mining is in crisis and I will try to restructure it," he said. "This is not an appeal for votes. But we cannot harbour hatred for ever."
